key_terms.meaning: A photon is removed when an atom or electron in a lower energy state moves to a higher state.
An excited atom emits a photon without an incoming photon; phase and direction are random.
An incoming photon triggers an excited atom to emit a second photon with the same phase, direction and wavelength.
More atoms or carriers occupy the upper laser level than the lower level, giving net optical gain.
Light is returned through the gain medium by mirrors or cleaved facets to build up oscillation.
The gain at which round-trip gain equals round-trip loss, so laser oscillation starts.
A forward-biased p-n junction that emits spontaneous light by carrier recombination.
Fraction of injected electrons that recombine radiatively, η<sub>int</sub> = radiative rate / total rate.
Fraction of generated light that escapes the chip rather than being absorbed or trapped.
Photons emitted outside the device per injected electron, η<sub>ext</sub> = η<sub>int</sub> η<sub>extract</sub>.
Optical power per unit emitting area per unit solid angle, in W/(m²·sr).
Two parallel reflecting facets that form a resonant cavity and select longitudinal modes.
A junction between two different semiconductor materials that confines carriers and light.
A thin active layer that quantises carrier energy levels and lowers laser threshold.
NA = √(n₁² − n₂²) for a step-index fiber; it sets the acceptance angle.
Ratio of power launched into the fiber to power emitted by the source, η<sub>c</sub> = P<sub>fiber</sub>/P<sub>source</sub>.
A sideways offset between two fiber cores that reduces overlap and adds loss.
An angle between fiber axes that sends light outside the acceptance cone and adds loss.
An end gap between fibers that causes beam spreading and Fresnel reflection loss.
An interferometer that converts a phase change into intensity modulation, often with I<sub>out</sub>/I<sub>in</sub> = cos²(Δφ/2).
λ(µm) = 1.24/E(eV); for a semiconductor source E ≈ E<sub>g</sub>
P<sub>int</sub> = η<sub>int</sub>(hc/qλ)I, with η<sub>int</sub> = τ/τ<sub>r</sub> and 1/τ = 1/τ<sub>r</sub> + 1/τ<sub>nr</sub>
η<sub>extraction</sub> ≈ 1/[n(n + 1)²], 1.3% for n = 3.6
Γg<sub>th</sub> = α<sub>i</sub> + (1/2L) ln[1/(R1R2)]; the second term is the mirror loss α<sub>m</sub>
Δν = c/(2n<sub>g</sub>L), Δλ = λ²/(2n<sub>g</sub>L)
P = η<sub>s</sub>(I − I<sub>th</sub>), η<sub>s</sub> = η<sub>d</sub>(hν/q) in W/A
η ≈ NA² for r<sub>s</sub> ≤ a; η ≈ (a/r<sub>s</sub>)²NA² for r<sub>s</sub> > a; P<sub>s</sub> = π²r<sub>s</sub>²B<sub>0</sub>
R = ((n<sub>1</sub> − n)/(n<sub>1</sub> + n))², loss −10 log₁₀(1 − R) per face
η = (2/π)[arccos x − x√(1 − x²)], x = d/(2a), step-index multimode
Vπ = λd/(2n³r<sub>33</sub>ΓL) for push-pull drive

takeaways: Absorption removes light, spontaneous emission gives incoherent light, and stimulated emission gives coherent light when a second photon triggers emission.
An LED is a spontaneous emitter; its launched power depends on internal quantum efficiency, extraction efficiency and coupling.
Laser oscillation requires population inversion, optical feedback and pump current above threshold gain.
A semiconductor laser diode uses cleaved facets as a Fabry-Perot cavity and emits coherent light above threshold current.
Heterojunctions and quantum wells shrink the active region, confine light and carriers, and reduce threshold current.
Source-to-fiber coupling efficiency depends on source radiance, fiber numerical aperture, core area and alignment.
Joint and connector losses from lateral, angular and longitudinal misalignment are added in dB.
A Mach-Zehnder modulator changes phase and then converts it to an intensity change with a cos²(Δφ/2) response.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine emission physics and laser threshold with device structure, power-launching calculations and dB loss accounting for joints and connectors.

bank.q: Explain absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission. Use simple energy-level diagrams and state why population inversion is needed for net optical gain.
outline: Define each of the three processes
Show lower and upper levels for each process
Spontaneous emission is random in phase and direction
Stimulated emission is coherent with the incoming photon
Absorption removes photons and opposes gain
Population inversion makes stimulated emission exceed absorption

answer.text: Model. Take a two-level system: lower level E1 with N1 atoms per m³ and upper level E2 with N2 per m³. Light of frequency f interacts only when hf = E2 − E1. For an 850 nm transition hf = 2.34×10⁻¹⁹ J = 1.46 eV. Let ρ(f) be the spectral energy density of the light in J m⁻³ Hz⁻¹.

svg.aria: Energy-level diagrams for absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission between levels E1 and E2.

answer: Absorption. A photon of energy hf is taken up and an electron moves from E1 to E2. The photon disappears, so absorption removes light from the beam. Its rate is B12ρ(f)N1 per m³ per second: it needs light and atoms in the lower level.

Spontaneous emission. An electron in E2 falls to E1 by itself, after a random delay whose average is the spontaneous lifetime τ<sub>sp</sub>, and emits one photon in a random direction with random phase. Its rate is A21N2, with A21 = 1/τ<sub>sp</sub>; for τ<sub>sp</sub> = 5 ns, A21 = 2.0×10⁸ s⁻¹. This incoherent light is what an LED gives.

Stimulated emission. A passing photon of energy hf makes an electron in E2 fall to E1 at once. The new photon has the same frequency, phase, direction and polarization as the trigger, so one photon in gives two identical photons out. Its rate is B21ρ(f)N2. This is the process a laser amplifies.

answer.text: Einstein relations. In thermal equilibrium the three rates must balance with blackbody radiation, which gives:
answer.pre:
B12 = B21                     (non-degenerate levels)
A21/B21 = 8πhf³/c³
N2/N1 = exp(−hf/kT)            (Boltzmann)

answer: Why inversion is needed. A beam gains photons from stimulated emission and loses them to absorption. With B12 = B21 the net gain rate is B21ρ(f)(N2 − N1), and the gain coefficient is g = σ(N2 − N1). The beam grows only if N2 > N1: more atoms in the upper level than in the lower. This is population inversion.

Why equilibrium cannot give it. At T = 300 K, kT = 4.14×10⁻²¹ J (0.0259 eV), so for 1.46 eV, hf/kT = 56.5 and N2/N1 = exp(−56.5) = 2.8×10⁻²⁵. The upper level is practically empty and absorption wins. The ratio of stimulated to spontaneous emission, 1/[exp(hf/kT) − 1], is also 2.8×10⁻²⁵, so thermal light is almost all spontaneous. Inversion must be forced by pumping.

In a semiconductor the pump is forward current. Electrons fill the conduction band and holes the valence band; inversion holds for photon energies between E<sub>g</sub> and the separation of the two quasi-Fermi levels, so the separation must exceed E<sub>g</sub>.

Closing check with numbers. If N2 = 2N1, the net stimulated rate is ∝ N2 − N1 = +N1, so light is amplified. If N2 = 0.5N1, absorption (∝ N1) is twice stimulated emission (∝ 0.5N1), and the beam is absorbed. Gain changes sign exactly at N2 = N1.

bank.q: Describe the structures of a surface-emitting LED and an edge-emitting LED. Compare their emission patterns, output power and suitability for fiber coupling.
outline: Forward-biased double-heterostructure junction emits by spontaneous recombination
Surface emitter radiates from a small circular area through the top or a substrate well
Edge emitter guides light along a stripe to a cleaved edge
Surface emitter has a wide Lambertian pattern
Edge emitter has a narrower, elliptical beam and couples better
Compare coupled power with η ≈ NA²
answer: Common base. Both are forward-biased double heterostructures: a thin active layer (GaAs for 0.85 µm, InGaAsP for 1.3 µm) between wider-bandgap p and n layers that hold the carriers. Injected electrons and holes recombine and emit spontaneously; there is no cavity and no threshold.

answer.text: Surface emitter. The active region is a small disc, about 50 µm across, defined by a small contact. Light leaves through the face parallel to the junction. In the Burrus type a well is etched through the substrate so the fiber end sits right on the emitting spot, held with index-matching epoxy. Edge emitter. The active layer sits between two guiding layers of lower index, under a stripe contact. The guide carries the light along the stripe and it leaves through the cleaved edge, from a strip a few micrometres high.

svg.aria: Two LED cross-sections. Left, a Burrus surface emitter: a fiber sits in a well etched in the substrate, right above a small active disc. Right, an edge emitter: a stripe contact over guide layers, with light leaving the cleaved edge in a narrower beam.

answer: Emission pattern. The surface emitter is Lambertian: intensity falls as cos θ, so the half-power beam width is 120° in every plane. The edge emitter is still about 120° wide in the plane of the junction, but the guide narrows it to roughly 25–35° in the perpendicular plane, so its beam is elliptical and more directional.
Radiance. The edge emitter puts its power into a small area and a smaller solid angle, so its radiance (W cm⁻² sr⁻¹) is higher, even though its total power can be similar or lower.

Coupling. For a Lambertian source no larger than the core, η ≈ NA². Into a fiber with NA = 0.20 that is 4%; if the source is larger than the core, η ≈ (a/r<sub>s</sub>)²NA² is smaller still. The edge emitter’s narrower beam puts more of its light inside the acceptance cone, so it couples several times more power into a small-core or low-NA fiber.

Output power. A flat surface emitter loses most of its internal light to total internal reflection: only 1/[n(n + 1)²] = 1.3% escapes for n = 3.6. Domes and index-matched epoxy raise this. Edge emitters lose light along the guide by absorption, but what remains is concentrated.

Closing check. The surface LED of the power-launching example (B<sub>0</sub> = 100 W cm⁻² sr⁻¹, r<sub>s</sub> = 35 µm) emits π²r<sub>s</sub>²B<sub>0</sub> = 12.1 mW but puts only 0.247 mW, 2.0%, into a 50 µm core of NA 0.20. That 2% is why edge emitters and lasers are preferred whenever more launched power is needed.

bank.q: Derive the threshold condition for laser oscillation in a Fabry-Perot cavity. Define threshold gain and explain how mirror loss enters the condition.
outline: Round-trip gain must equal round-trip loss
Use facet reflectivities R1 and R2, cavity length L, internal loss α<sub>i</sub> and confinement factor Γ
Threshold gain Γg<sub>th</sub> = α<sub>i</sub> + (1/(2L))ln(1/(R1R2))
Mirror loss increases when reflectivity falls or the cavity is shorter
Threshold current is the current needed to reach g<sub>th</sub>
Oscillation starts at a resonant longitudinal mode, 2nL = mλ
answer: Set-up. A Fabry–Perot cavity of length L has facets of power reflectance R1 and R2. The medium has material gain g (per cm) when pumped, of which only the fraction Γ in the active layer acts on the mode, so the modal gain is Γg. The internal loss α<sub>i</sub> (scattering, free-carrier absorption) acts all along the path.

answer.text: Follow the intensity for one round trip, starting with I0 just inside facet 1:
answer.pre:
after travelling L:          I0·exp[(Γg − αi)L]
after reflection at facet 2: I0·R2·exp[(Γg − αi)L]
back at facet 1:             I0·R2·exp[2(Γg − αi)L]
after reflection at facet 1: I0·R1R2·exp[2(Γg − αi)L]

answer.text: Threshold. Oscillation is self-sustaining when the light comes back with the same intensity, so the round-trip factor is 1:
answer.pre:
R1R2·exp[2L(Γg<sub>th</sub> − αi)] = 1
2L(Γg<sub>th</sub> − αi) = ln[1/(R1R2)]
Γg<sub>th</sub> = αi + (1/2L)·ln[1/(R1R2)] = αi + αm

answer: Definitions. g<sub>th</sub> is the threshold material gain; Γg<sub>th</sub> is the threshold modal gain. αm = (1/2L)ln[1/(R1R2)] is the mirror loss, the light that leaves through the facets spread over the cavity length. Below threshold any gain is used up by losses; above it the gain clamps at g<sub>th</sub> and every extra electron adds output.

How mirror loss enters. Lower reflectance gives a larger ln[1/(R1R2)], so a larger αm and a higher threshold. A longer cavity spreads the same facet loss over more length, so αm falls as 1/L. A high-reflection coat on the rear facet cuts αm and sends most light out of the front. Mirror loss is not wasted: it is the useful output.
Phase condition. The round trip must also return the wave in phase: 2nL = mλ for an integer m. Only these longitudinal modes can oscillate, spaced Δν = c/(2n<sub>g</sub>L) apart.

From gain to current. In the linear-gain model g = βJ, so the threshold current density is J<sub>th</sub> = (α<sub>i</sub> + α<sub>m</sub>)/(Γβ) and I<sub>th</sub> = J<sub>th</sub> × (stripe width × L). Above threshold P = η<sub>s</sub>(I − I<sub>th</sub>).

answer.text: Numbers for L = 300 µm, R1 = R2 = 0.32, α<sub>i</sub> = 10 cm⁻¹, Γ = 0.30, n<sub>g</sub> = 3.6:

answer: Closing check. Coat the rear facet to R2 = 0.90: R1R2 = 0.288, ln(1/0.288) = 1.245, α<sub>m</sub> = 1.245/0.06 = 20.75 cm⁻¹ and Γg<sub>th</sub> = 30.75 cm⁻¹, a 36% lower threshold gain, as the formula predicts for higher reflectance.

bank.q: Explain internal quantum efficiency, extraction efficiency and external quantum efficiency of an LED. Show how each reduces the power available at the fiber.
outline: Define η<sub>int</sub> as the radiative fraction of recombination, τ/τ<sub>r</sub>
Define η<sub>extraction</sub> as the fraction escaping the chip
Define η<sub>ext</sub> = η<sub>int</sub>η<sub>extraction</sub>
Non-radiative recombination wastes injected carriers
Total internal reflection and Fresnel reflection trap light
Fiber coupling η ≈ NA² reduces power further
answer: The chain. Current I injects I/q electrons per second. Each can give at most one photon of energy hc/λ, so the upper limit of optical power is (hc/qλ)I. Three factors then cut it: internal efficiency, extraction efficiency and fiber coupling.

Internal quantum efficiency. A carrier recombines radiatively (lifetime τ<sub>r</sub>) or non-radiatively at defects and surfaces (τ<sub>nr</sub>). The total lifetime is 1/τ = 1/τ<sub>r</sub> + 1/τ<sub>nr</sub>, and η<sub>int</sub> = τ/τ<sub>r</sub>, the photons made per electron. Internal power: P<sub>int</sub> = η<sub>int</sub>(hc/qλ)I.

Extraction efficiency. Photons are made inside a material of index n ≈ 3.6. Only rays within the critical angle θ<sub>c</sub> = sin⁻¹(1/n) = 16.1° of the normal can leave a flat face; the rest are totally reflected and mostly reabsorbed. Fresnel reflection takes part of the escaping cone too. For a flat face into air, η<sub>extraction</sub> ≈ 1/[n(n + 1)²].

External quantum efficiency. η<sub>ext</sub> = η<sub>int</sub> × η<sub>extraction</sub> is the photons leaving the chip per injected electron. It is different from the power (wall-plug) efficiency P<sub>out</sub>/(IV), which also counts the electrical drop.
Fiber coupling. A Lambertian source no larger than the core couples η<sub>c</sub> ≈ NA² of its emitted power; larger sources lose a further (a/r<sub>s</sub>)².

answer.text: Numbers: 0.85 µm LED, τ<sub>r</sub> = 50 ns, τ<sub>nr</sub> = 80 ns, I = 30 mA, V = 1.6 V, n = 3.6, fiber NA = 0.20 with the source smaller than the core:

answer: Efficiencies from the table: η<sub>ext</sub> = 0.615 × 0.0131 = 0.0081 (0.81%). Electrical input is 0.030 × 1.6 = 48 mW, so the wall-plug efficiency is 0.354/48 = 0.74%.

Which loss is largest. Extraction (−18.8 dB) dwarfs the internal loss (−2.1 dB); coupling adds −14.0 dB. That is why LED design concentrates on domes, textured surfaces, epoxy lenses and the Burrus well.
Closing check. Overall 0.615 × 0.0131 × 0.04 = 3.23×10⁻⁴; 3.23×10⁻⁴ × 43.9 mW = 14.2 µW, the same as the table. In dB: 10 log₁₀(14.2 µW / 43.9 mW) = −34.9 dB, which equals −2.1 − 18.8 − 14.0.

bank.q: A surface-emitting LED has radiance B<sub>0</sub> = 60 W cm⁻² sr⁻¹ and an emitting diameter of 50 µm. Find its total emitted power and the power coupled into (a) a step-index fiber with 62.5 µm core and NA = 0.275, and (b) a step-index fiber with 50 µm core and NA = 0.20. Give each coupling loss in dB and the power left after Fresnel reflection at a fiber face of index 1.47.
outline: Lambertian source: P<sub>s</sub> = π²r<sub>s</sub>²B<sub>0</sub> with r in cm
Compare r<sub>s</sub> with the core radius a
r<sub>s</sub> ≤ a, so P = P<sub>s</sub>NA²
Coupling loss = −10 log₁₀(P/P<sub>s</sub>)
Fresnel R = ((n<sub>1</sub> − 1)/(n<sub>1</sub> + 1))²
Compare the two fibers
answer: Data in consistent units: r<sub>s</sub> = 25 µm = 2.5×10⁻³ cm; fiber (a) a = 31.25 µm, NA = 0.275; fiber (b) a = 25 µm, NA = 0.20; B<sub>0</sub> = 60 W cm⁻² sr⁻¹.

answer.text: Total emitted power of the Lambertian surface:

answer: Fiber (a): r<sub>s</sub> = 25 µm ≤ a = 31.25 µm, so the whole source sits within the core and P = P<sub>s</sub>NA² = 3.70 mW × 0.275² = 3.70 × 0.0756 = 0.280 mW. Loss = −10 log₁₀(0.0756) = 11.2 dB.
Fiber (b): r<sub>s</sub> = a = 25 µm, still the small-source case, so P = 3.70 mW × 0.20² = 3.70 × 0.04 = 0.148 mW. Loss = −10 log₁₀(0.04) = 14.0 dB.
Fresnel reflection at the fiber face: R = ((1.47 − 1)/(1.47 + 1))² = (0.47/2.47)² = 0.0362, so the face passes 0.9638 (0.16 dB).

Why fiber (a) wins: η depends on NA², and (0.275/0.20)² = 1.89, so it collects 1.89 times the power, a 2.8 dB advantage. The larger core does not help here because the source already fits inside both cores.
Closing check: 0.280/0.148 = 1.89 ✓ and 14.0 − 11.2 = 2.8 dB ✓. If the source radius were 50 µm, fiber (b) would also lose (25/50)² = 0.25, another 6.0 dB.

bank.q: Two step-index multimode fibers with core radius 25 µm, NA = 0.20 and core index 1.48 are joined in air with a lateral offset of 5 µm, a tilt of 2° and an end gap of 5 µm. Find each loss, the total joint loss in dB and the fraction of power that passes. How would a fusion splice change the result?
outline: Lateral: η = (2/π)[arccos x − x√(1 − x²)], x = d/(2a)
Angular: L = −10 log₁₀[1 − nθ/(πNA)], θ in radians
Gap: L = −10 log₁₀[a/(a + s tan θ<sub>c</sub>)]², θ<sub>c</sub> = sin⁻¹(NA/n)
Fresnel: two glass–air faces
dB losses add
Fusion splice removes the gap and the faces
answer: End gap: θ<sub>c</sub> = sin⁻¹(0.20/1.0) = 11.54°, tan θ<sub>c</sub> = 0.2041; s tan θ<sub>c</sub> = 5 × 0.2041 = 1.02 µm; a/(a + s tan θ<sub>c</sub>) = 25/26.02 = 0.9608; squared 0.9231; L<sub>gap</sub> = 0.35 dB.
Fresnel: R = ((1.48 − 1)/(1.48 + 1))² = (0.48/2.48)² = 0.0375. Each face passes 0.9625 (0.166 dB); there are two faces, so L<sub>F</sub> = 0.33 dB.

Why the dB values add: each cause multiplies the power by its fraction, and the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms. Total 0.59 + 0.25 + 0.35 + 0.33 = 1.52 dB, so the joint passes 10<sup>−0.152</sup> = 0.705, about 70% of the light.
Largest term. The lateral offset dominates even though it is only a tenth of the core diameter; tilt is the smallest because 2° is small next to the 11.5° acceptance half-angle.

Fusion splice. The arc melts the two ends together: there is no gap and no glass–air face, so the gap and Fresnel terms vanish, and surface tension pulls the cores into line during fusion. A good fusion splice loses under 0.1 dB, against 1.52 dB here.

Index-matching gel instead (n = 1.48): the Fresnel loss vanishes and θ<sub>c</sub> falls to 7.77°, so the gap loss falls to 0.23 dB; the tilt term rises to 0.37 dB because the formula has n in it. The joint then loses 0.59 + 0.37 + 0.23 = 1.20 dB.
Closing check: product of fractions 0.873 × 0.944 × 0.923 × 0.926 = 0.705, and −10 log₁₀(0.705) = 1.52 dB ✓.

bank.q: A push-pull Mach-Zehnder modulator has Vπ = 5 V. Find the output intensity ratio at V = 2.5 V and V = 5 V using I<sub>out</sub>/I<sub>in</sub> = cos²(πV/(2Vπ)), the voltage that gives 90% transmission, the small-signal slope at quadrature, and the extinction ratio if the splitter divides the power 55:45.
outline: Push-pull phase difference Δφ = πV/Vπ
V = 2.5 V gives cos²(π/4) = 0.5 (quadrature)
V = 5 V gives cos²(π/2) = 0, the first null
Solve cos²(πV/10) = 0.9 for V
Slope (π/2Vπ) sin(πV/Vπ) is largest at quadrature
ER = ((a + b)/(a − b))² for unequal arms
answer: Transfer function: with Δφ = πV/Vπ, the output is I<sub>out</sub>/I<sub>in</sub> = cos²(Δφ/2) = cos²(πV/(2Vπ)) = cos²(πV/10) for Vπ = 5 V.
At V = 2.5 V: πV/10 = π/4, cos²(π/4) = 0.5. Half the light passes; this is the quadrature point.
At V = 5 V: πV/10 = π/2, cos²(π/2) = 0. The arms are π out of phase and cancel: the first null, which is what defines Vπ.
For 90% transmission: cos(πV/10) = √0.9 = 0.9487, so πV/10 = 0.3218 rad and V = 1.02 V.

answer.pre:
d(I<sub>out</sub>/I<sub>in</sub>)/dV = −(π/2Vπ)·sin(πV/Vπ)
at V = 2.5 V: sin(π/2) = 1, slope magnitude = π/10 = 0.314 per volt

answer: So a ±0.1 V signal at quadrature swings the output by about ±0.031 of I<sub>in</sub>, roughly ±3%. At V = 0 or 5 V the slope is zero, so a small signal there gives almost no modulation; hence the quadrature bias for analog and small-signal use.

Extinction ratio with a 55:45 splitter: the arm field amplitudes are a = √0.55 = 0.742 and b = √0.45 = 0.671. P<sub>max</sub> ∝ (a + b)² = 1.995 and P<sub>min</sub> ∝ (a − b)² = 0.00501, so ER = 1.995/0.00501 = 398, that is 26.0 dB. The null is no longer zero.
For on-off keying, drive between V = 0 (on) and V = Vπ = 5 V (off): a 5 V swing, or 2.5 V on each arm in push-pull.
Closing check: 0.5 at 2.5 V and 0 at 5 V ✓; cos²(π × 1.02/10) = cos²(0.320) = 0.90 ✓; 10 log₁₀(398) = 26.0 dB ✓.

bank.q: An LED is driven at 50 mA with a forward voltage of 1.8 V. Its external quantum efficiency is 2% and it emits at 850 nm. Find the emitted optical power, the photons per second, the wall-plug efficiency, and the power coupled into a fiber with 5% coupling efficiency in mW and dBm.
outline: Photon energy hc/λ = 2.34×10⁻¹⁹ J (1.4625 eV)
Electrons per second I/q
Emitted photons = η<sub>ext</sub> × I/q
P<sub>out</sub> = η<sub>ext</sub>(hc/qλ)I
Wall-plug efficiency = P<sub>out</sub>/(IV)
Coupled power = 0.05 × P<sub>out</sub>; dBm = 10 log₁₀(P/1 mW)
answer: Electrons injected: I/q = 0.050/(1.60×10⁻¹⁹) = 3.125×10¹⁷ s⁻¹.
Photons leaving the LED: η<sub>ext</sub> × I/q = 0.02 × 3.125×10¹⁷ = 6.25×10¹⁵ s⁻¹.

Electrical input: IV = 0.050 × 1.8 = 0.090 W = 90 mW. Wall-plug efficiency = 1.46/90 = 0.0163, that is 1.6%. It is lower than η<sub>ext</sub> = 2% because each electron carries 1.8 eV of electrical energy but its photon only 1.46 eV.
A common mistake is to take 2% of the 90 mW electrical power, giving 1.8 mW. That treats a quantum (photon per electron) efficiency as a power efficiency and is wrong by the factor 1.8/1.4625 = 1.23.
Coupled power: 0.05 × 1.46 mW = 0.0731 mW = 73.1 µW. In dBm: 10 log₁₀(0.0731) = −11.4 dBm.
Assumption: the 2% already includes extraction from the chip, so it is applied once; coupling is a separate factor that depends on the fiber NA and the source size.
Closing check: 1.46 mW in dBm is +1.65 dBm; a 5% coupling is −13.0 dB; +1.65 − 13.0 = −11.4 dBm ✓.

bank.q: An InGaAsP Fabry-Perot laser at 1.55 µm has an uncoated cavity 250 µm long with refractive index 3.5, internal loss 20 cm⁻¹, confinement factor 0.25 and group index 3.7. Its threshold current is 15 mA and its differential quantum efficiency is 0.35. Find the facet reflectance, mirror loss, threshold modal and material gain, the longitudinal mode spacing in nm and GHz, the slope efficiency, and the output power at 45 mA.
outline: α<sub>m</sub> = (1/2L)ln[1/(R1R2)] with L in cm
Γg<sub>th</sub> = α<sub>i</sub> + α<sub>m</sub>; g<sub>th</sub> = Γg<sub>th</sub>/Γ
Δλ = λ²/(2n<sub>g</sub>L), Δν = c/(2n<sub>g</sub>L)
η<sub>s</sub> = η<sub>d</sub>(hν/q)
P = η<sub>s</sub>(I − I<sub>th</sub>)
answer: Facet reflectance: R = ((3.5 − 1)/(3.5 + 1))² = (2.5/4.5)² = 0.309 for each uncoated cleaved facet.

Threshold gain: Γg<sub>th</sub> = α<sub>i</sub> + α<sub>m</sub> = 20 + 47.0 = 67.0 cm⁻¹ (modal). The material must give g<sub>th</sub> = 67.0/0.25 = 268 cm⁻¹ because only a quarter of the mode overlaps the active layer.
With a gain band about 30 nm wide, roughly 30/1.30 = 23 longitudinal modes can lase: a multimode spectrum, which is why long links use single-mode DFB lasers.
Slope efficiency: hν/q = 1.24/1.55 = 0.800 V, so η<sub>s</sub> = η<sub>d</sub>(hν/q) = 0.35 × 0.800 = 0.280 W/A.
Trap avoided: using the whole current gives 0.280 × 0.045 = 12.6 mW, which ignores that the first 15 mA only brings the gain up to threshold.
Closing check: Δλ and Δν agree, since Δλ = λ²Δν/c = (1.55×10⁻⁶)² × 1.62×10¹¹/3.00×10⁸ = 1.30 nm ✓; mirror loss is 70% of the total 67 cm⁻¹, so this short uncoated cavity is mirror-loss dominated.

bank.q: Compare a heterojunction laser and a quantum-well laser in terms of carrier confinement, optical confinement, threshold current density, wavelength control and temperature sensitivity.
outline: Heterojunction confines carriers by the bandgap step
It confines light by the refractive-index step (confinement factor Γ)
Quantum well adds size quantisation of the energy levels
Quantum well gives lower threshold current density
Quantum well tunes wavelength by well width
Compare temperature stability and fabrication complexity
answer: Structures. A double-heterostructure (DH) laser has a bulk active layer about 0.1–0.2 µm thick, for example GaAs between Al<sub>x</sub>Ga<sub>1−x</sub>As claddings. A quantum-well (QW) laser thins the active layer to about 5–20 nm, so thin that electron motion across it is quantised; it usually adds separate-confinement layers to guide the light.

Carrier confinement. In both, the cladding bandgap is higher, so the step stops carriers diffusing away. For x = 0.30 the cladding has E<sub>g</sub> = 1.424 + 1.266(0.30) + 0.266(0.09) = 1.828 eV against 1.424 eV for GaAs, a 0.40 eV barrier. The QW confines in a much smaller volume, so the same current gives a far higher carrier density.

Optical confinement. The index step (about 0.2–0.3 for GaAs/AlGaAs) guides the mode. In a bulk DH, Γ is a few tenths. A single 10 nm well is far thinner than the mode, so Γ is only about 0.01–0.05; QW lasers recover it with a separate-confinement heterostructure to hold the light and several wells (MQW) to add gain.

Threshold current density. The QW density of states is step-like, so the gain rises steeply once the first level fills, and the volume to invert is tiny. Typical J<sub>th</sub> falls by a factor of two or more compared with a DH laser, to a few hundred A/cm². Strain lowers it further by reducing the hole mass.

answer.text: Wavelength control. In a DH the wavelength is set by the material bandgap only. In a QW the confined levels add to the gap, so the well width tunes the wavelength. For a 10 nm GaAs well:

answer: Temperature sensitivity. Threshold rises with temperature as I<sub>th</sub> ∝ exp(T/T<sub>c</sub>). Better carrier confinement keeps fewer carriers escaping over the barriers, so well-designed QW and strained-QW lasers keep T<sub>c</sub> higher; long-wavelength InGaAsP devices still have T<sub>c</sub> of only 50–70 K and often need a cooler.

head: Feature
Double heterostructure
Quantum well
rows: small per well; SCH and MQW restore it

answer: Verdict. The QW laser wins on threshold, wavelength control and efficiency, at the price of tighter growth control. Almost every modern telecom laser uses MQW active regions.

Closing check. Halving the well to 5 nm multiplies E<sub>1e</sub> by 4 to 0.225 eV, shifting the emission further to shorter wavelength; widening it reduces the shift towards the bulk 871 nm, as E ∝ 1/L² predicts.

bank.q: Choose a source for a short 100 m indoor link and a 10 km metro link. Compare LED and semiconductor laser on spectrum, output power, coupling, threshold, cost and reliability. Justify each choice.
outline: LED has broad spectrum and low coherence
Laser has narrow spectrum and coherent output
LED is cheap and reliable but couples poorly
Laser gives higher launched power and better fiber coupling
Short link can tolerate LED spectrum and lower power
Long link needs a laser for power and dispersion budget
answer: Spectrum. An 850 nm LED has a spectral width of about 40 nm because it emits by spontaneous recombination across a spread of carrier energies. A Fabry–Perot laser emits a few longitudinal modes spread over a few nm (1.3 nm apart for the 250 µm cavity); a DFB laser emits one mode, well under 1 nm wide.

Output and coupled power. An LED emits a few mW, but as a Lambertian source it couples only about NA² of it: 4% into an NA 0.20 multimode fiber (0.15–0.25 mW in the coupling examples) and far less into single-mode fiber. A laser beam is narrow, so a lensed laser launches 1–10 mW into single-mode fiber.

Modulation speed. An LED’s speed is set by the carrier lifetime: τ = 30.8 ns gives an electrical bandwidth 1/(2πτ) = 5.2 MHz, and fast LEDs reach a few hundred MHz. Stimulated emission is much faster, so lasers modulate at Gb/s rates.

Threshold and drive. An LED has no threshold and an almost linear P-I line, so a simple current drive works. A laser needs I > I<sub>th</sub>, a bias circuit and usually a monitor photodiode, because I<sub>th</sub> drifts with temperature as exp(T/T<sub>c</sub>).

Cost and reliability. LEDs are cheaper, simpler and longer-lived, and are much less sensitive to temperature and to light reflected back into them. Lasers cost more, need heat sinking and sometimes isolators and coolers.

answer.text: Dispersion check for the 100 m link, using multimode fiber at 850 nm with |D| = 90 ps/(nm·km) taken as given:

answer: A 360 ps spread allows NRZ rates of the order of 1 Gb/s, far above what a room link of 10–100 Mb/s needs. The LED’s loss budget is also easy: 100 m of fiber at about 3 dB/km loses only 0.3 dB.

10 km metro link. Now the link needs single-mode fiber at 1310 or 1550 nm for bandwidth over distance. An LED cannot put useful power into a 9 µm core, and a 40 nm-wide spectrum over 10 km would spread pulses by nanoseconds. A laser launches milliwatts into single-mode fiber and its narrow line keeps dispersion small, so a laser (DFB at higher rates) is the choice.

head: Feature
LED
Laser diode
Matters most for
rows: MHz to a few hundred MHz

answer: Verdict. 100 m indoor link: an 850 nm LED on multimode fiber, because cost, simplicity and reliability matter and its spectrum, power and speed are more than enough. 10 km metro link: a 1310 or 1550 nm laser diode on single-mode fiber, because only a laser gives the launched power, narrow spectrum and speed the distance demands.
Closing check. The LED’s 360 ps spread over 100 m would become 3.6 ns per 1 km of the same fiber, already a limit at a few hundred Mb/s, which confirms that the LED belongs to the short link.

bank.q: Analyze how lateral offset, angular tilt, longitudinal gap and NA mismatch each produce loss at a fiber joint. Explain why losses are added in dB and describe two practical ways to reduce them.
outline: Lateral offset reduces core overlap
Angular tilt sends rays outside the acceptance cone
Longitudinal gap spreads the beam and adds Fresnel loss
NA mismatch leaves some launched rays unguided
dB losses add because power fractions multiply
Use fusion splicing, precision ferrules and index-matching gel
answer: Classify first. Extrinsic losses come from how the ends are held (lateral offset, tilt, gap, end finish); intrinsic losses come from the fibers themselves (core size, NA, profile). Each is a power fraction η, quoted as −10 log₁₀ η dB.

Lateral offset d. The two core circles overlap only partly, and light from the non-overlapping area goes into the cladding. For step-index fibers with uniform launch, η = (2/π)[arccos x − x√(1 − x²)] with x = d/(2a). For a 50 µm core with d = 10 µm, x = 0.2 and η = 0.747, a 1.27 dB loss: the most sensitive error.

Angular tilt θ. The cone leaving one fiber is tilted relative to the acceptance cone of the next, so its edge falls outside. L<sub>ang</sub> = −10 log₁₀[1 − nθ/(πNA)]: a 1° tilt (0.01745 rad) with NA = 0.20 in air costs 0.12 dB. Larger NA makes the joint more tolerant.

Longitudinal gap s. Light spreads at the cone half-angle θ<sub>c</sub> = sin⁻¹(NA/n) across the gap, so part of it lands outside the far core: L<sub>gap</sub> = −10 log₁₀[a/(a + s tan θ<sub>c</sub>)]². A 10 µm gap in air with a = 25 µm and NA = 0.20 costs 0.68 dB. The gap also creates two glass–air faces with Fresnel reflection R = ((1.48 − 1)/(1.48 + 1))² = 0.0375 each, 0.33 dB for both.

NA mismatch. If the receiving fiber has a smaller NA, rays steeper than its acceptance angle are not guided: loss ≈ −10 log₁₀(NA<sub>R</sub>/NA<sub>E</sub>)², so 0.20 into 0.18 costs 0.92 dB. Into a larger NA there is no loss. Core-size mismatch works the same way with (a<sub>R</sub>/a<sub>E</sub>)²: 62.5 µm into 50 µm costs 1.94 dB.

Why losses add in dB. Each cause passes a fraction of what reaches it, so the total fraction is the product η<sub>1</sub>η<sub>2</sub>η<sub>3</sub>…; since log(ab) = log a + log b, the dB losses add. For example, two joints each passing 0.9 lose 0.458 dB each: 0.915 dB in all, and 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81 gives the same 0.915 dB.

Reduction method 1: fusion splicing. Melting the ends together removes the gap and both faces, and surface tension self-aligns the cores; losses fall below 0.1 dB. Mechanical splices with V-grooves and index gel are quicker but typically lose more.

Reduction method 2: precision connectors. Ceramic ferrules of 2.5 mm (SC, ST) or 1.25 mm (LC) hold the fiber to about a micrometre, physical-contact polish closes the gap, and an 8° angled polish (APC) sends reflections out of the core for high return loss. Index-matching gel in a mechanical joint removes the Fresnel loss but cannot fix an offset.
Closing check. The 1.27 dB offset alone is larger than the gap, tilt and Fresnel terms together (0.68 + 0.12 + 0.33 = 1.13 dB), which is why alignment of the cores matters most.

bank.q: Compare direct modulation of a laser diode with external Mach-Zehnder modulation for high-bit-rate links. Discuss chirp, extinction ratio, bias control and insertion loss.
outline: Direct modulation changes the laser current
It causes chirp and relaxation effects
External modulator keeps the laser at constant bias
Mach-Zehnder gives low chirp and a high extinction ratio
External modulator adds insertion loss and needs bias control
Choose by reach, bit rate and cost
answer: Direct modulation. The data current is added to a bias above threshold, and output follows P = η<sub>s</sub>(I − I<sub>th</sub>). No extra optical part is needed, so it is cheap and compact.

Chirp. Changing the current changes the carrier density, and with it the refractive index, so the laser frequency swings during each pulse. The chirped pulse has a wider spectrum, and fiber dispersion turns that into pulse spreading; this, not the laser’s speed, limits directly modulated links at 10 Gb/s and above over long fiber.

Extinction ratio of direct modulation. To avoid turn-on delay and the worst chirp the laser is kept above threshold in the off state. For I<sub>th</sub> = 20 mA and η<sub>s</sub> = 0.30 W/A, driving between 25 mA and 60 mA gives 1.5 mW and 12 mW: ER = 10 log₁₀(12/1.5) = 9.0 dB.

External Mach-Zehnder modulation. The laser runs CW at constant current, so its line stays narrow; the MZM sets the intensity through P<sub>out</sub> = P<sub>in</sub>cos²(πV/2Vπ). In push-pull drive the two arm phases change in opposite directions and the common phase cancels, so the output is nearly chirp-free.

Extinction ratio of the MZM. The null is set by the splitter balance: a 55:45 split gives P<sub>max</sub>/P<sub>min</sub> = ((0.742 + 0.671)/(0.742 − 0.671))² = 398, i.e. 26 dB, far better than the 9 dB above.

Bias control. The MZM must sit at a set point (quadrature or the null) on a cos² curve that drifts with temperature and charge build-up in LiNbO<sub>3</sub>, so it needs a feedback bias loop. The laser in direct modulation needs bias tracking because I<sub>th</sub> drifts as exp(T/T<sub>c</sub>).

Drive voltage and insertion loss. A LiNbO<sub>3</sub> MZM with d = 10 µm, L = 2 cm and Γ = 0.5 has Vπ = λd/(2n³r<sub>33</sub>ΓL) = 2.57 V in push-pull, so it needs a broadband driver of a few volts. Waveguide and fiber-coupling losses add a few dB of insertion loss, which the power budget must cover, and the device is centimetres long.

head: Property
Direct modulation
External MZM
rows: 26 dB for a 55:45 split, higher when balanced
set point on cos² curve, feedback loop
short reach, up to about 10 Gb/s

answer: Verdict. Direct modulation suits short and metro links and cost-sensitive access networks, where reach is short enough that chirp does little harm. External MZM modulation is preferred for long-haul and high-rate links, and for the phase-coded formats of coherent systems, because only it gives clean, low-chirp pulses with a high extinction ratio.

Closing check. Raising the direct-modulation off level to 30 mA gives 3 mW and ER = 10 log₁₀(12/3) = 6.0 dB, showing the trade: more bias means less chirp and turn-on delay but a poorer extinction ratio.

bank.q: Trace the steps from carrier injection to coherent output in a semiconductor laser: emission processes, population inversion, gain, feedback, threshold and heterojunction confinement. Explain what limits the output power.
outline: Forward bias injects electrons and holes into the active layer
Recombination gives spontaneous and stimulated emission
Population inversion gives net gain
Cleaved facets provide optical feedback
Oscillation starts above threshold gain and threshold current
Heterojunction confines carriers and light
Output power is limited by heating, gain saturation and facet damage
answer: Injection. Forward bias drives electrons from the n-side and holes from the p-side into a thin active layer. In a double heterostructure the wider-gap claddings (for GaAs/Al<sub>0.30</sub>Ga<sub>0.70</sub>As, 1.828 eV against 1.424 eV) stop them leaving, so the carrier density builds until recombination balances injection.

Spontaneous emission first. At low current the carriers recombine spontaneously, each emitting a photon of energy close to E<sub>g</sub> in a random direction: λ = 1.24/1.424 = 0.871 µm for bulk GaAs. The device behaves like an LED, giving microwatts.

Population inversion. As the density rises, the quasi-Fermi levels separate. Once their separation exceeds the photon energy, more states are filled at the upper energy than at the lower, which is inversion. Stimulated emission now beats absorption and the medium has gain g, roughly g = βJ in the linear model.
Optical confinement. The claddings also have a lower index, so the layer is a waveguide; a fraction Γ of the mode overlaps the gain, and the modal gain is Γg.

Feedback. The cleaved facets reflect R = ((3.5 − 1)/(3.5 + 1))² = 0.31 each, forming a Fabry–Perot cavity. Photons from spontaneous emission travelling along the axis are amplified by stimulated emission on each pass, reflect, and return.

answer.text: Threshold. Oscillation starts when the round-trip gain equals the losses:
answer.pre:
R1R2·exp[2L(Γg<sub>th</sub> − αi)] = 1  →  Γg<sub>th</sub> = αi + (1/2L)·ln[1/(R1R2)]
L = 300 µm, R = 0.32, αi = 10 cm⁻¹, Γ = 0.30:
αm = 37.98 cm⁻¹,  Γg<sub>th</sub> = 47.98 cm⁻¹,  g<sub>th</sub> = 159.9 cm⁻¹

answer: Coherent output. Above threshold the gain clamps at g<sub>th</sub>; each extra electron gives a stimulated photon that copies the existing field, so the output is narrow-band and directional, in modes 2nL = mλ spaced c/(2n<sub>g</sub>L) = 139 GHz apart for n<sub>g</sub> = 3.6. The light-current line is P = η<sub>s</sub>(I − I<sub>th</sub>).

answer.text: Numbers for I<sub>th</sub> = 20 mA, η<sub>s</sub> = 0.30 W/A, V = 1.8 V:

answer: What limits the output power. (1) Heating: 96 of the 108 mW at 60 mA becomes heat; temperature raises I<sub>th</sub> as exp(T/T<sub>c</sub>), lowers η<sub>s</sub>, and the L-I curve bends over (thermal rollover). (2) Gain saturation and spatial hole burning at high photon density, which make the output kink and go multimode. (3) Catastrophic optical damage: the facet absorbs light, heats and melts above a power density limit; coatings and wider stripes raise it. (4) Lifetime: high current and temperature speed up degradation.

Role of confinement in the trace. Because carriers and light share the same thin layer, threshold falls; quantum wells (5–20 nm) go further by quantising the levels, which lowers J<sub>th</sub> again and shifts λ (833 nm for a 10 nm GaAs well).
Closing check. At 60 mA, P = 0.30 × (0.060 − 0.020) = 12.0 mW ✓, and the differential quantum efficiency at 0.85 µm would be η<sub>d</sub> = 0.30/(1.24/0.85) = 0.21, well below 1 as it must be.

glossary.def: Loss of a photon when an electron or atom moves from a lower to a higher energy state.
Random emission of a photon by an excited atom without an incoming photon.
Emission of a photon coherent with an incoming photon when the atom is already excited.
Condition where the upper energy level has more carriers than the lower level, so stimulated emission exceeds absorption.
Return of part of the light to the gain medium by mirrors or facets to sustain laser oscillation.
Gain that makes round-trip gain equal round-trip loss and starts laser action.
Semiconductor region where carriers recombine and light is generated or amplified.
Fraction of injected carriers that recombine radiatively.
Fraction of generated light that leaves the chip.
Photons emitted outside the device per injected electron.
Power emitted per unit area per unit solid angle, in W/(m²·sr).
Source whose radiance is constant with angle and whose intensity falls as cos θ.
Two parallel mirrors, such as cleaved facets, that provide optical feedback at resonant wavelengths.
Mirror-like end face formed by cleaving a semiconductor crystal along a crystal plane.
Junction of two semiconductors with different band gaps that can confine carriers and light.
Very thin semiconductor layer that confines carriers and creates quantised energy levels.
NA = √(n₁² − n₂²) for step-index fiber; it measures the light-gathering cone.
Ratio of power launched into the fiber to power emitted by the source.
Sideways offset between two fiber cores.
Angle between the axes of two fibers.
Gap between fiber ends along the axis.
Loss added by a component, in dB, equal to 10 log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P<sub>out</sub>).
Two-path interferometer that converts phase difference into intensity change.
Ratio of high to low optical power in a modulated signal.
Changing laser drive current to modulate output power.
Fraction Γ of the optical mode power that lies in the active layer; modal gain is Γg.
Extra output photons per extra injected electron above threshold, η<sub>d</sub> = η<sub>s</sub>q/(hν).
T<sub>c</sub> in I<sub>th</sub> ∝ exp(T/T<sub>c</sub>); a small T<sub>c</sub> means a strongly temperature-sensitive laser.
Reflected power below the incident power, in dB, −10 log₁₀(R); a high value means little reflection.
Vπ, the drive voltage that changes the phase difference between the two arms of a Mach-Zehnder modulator by π.
